The big idea in 30 seconds

Immune cells have no eyes. They recognize what to attack by contact, checking the protein fragments that nearly every cell displays on its surface. That explains how the immune system can protect you from cancer, why it sometimes fails, and how the newest cancer treatments work.

The chapters

Twelve chapters in three parts

Part I explains how the immune system works, Part II what cancer is and how it evades the immune system, and Part III the treatments that turn the immune system against it. Each chapter builds on the ones before it, so they read best in order.

Part I

The Immune System

The cells and molecules of immunity, and how they distinguish the body’s own cells from everything else.

5 chapters · about 2 hours

  1. 1 Chapter 1 Cells, Proteins and Molecular Recognition Cells, genes, proteins and molecular binding: the basic biology behind every act of immune recognition. 23 min
  2. 2 Chapter 2 Innate Immunity Within minutes of a splinter, your body mounts a defense against bacteria it has never encountered and never needs to identify. 23 min
  3. 3 Chapter 3 Adaptive Immunity The body makes millions of random receptors in advance, then multiplies the cells whose receptors bind a new pathogen. 27 min
  4. 4 Chapter 4 Antigen Presentation Nearly every cell displays samples of the proteins it makes inside, which is how T cells tell healthy cells from infected or mutated ones. 26 min
  5. 5 Chapter 5 T Cells: Selection, Killing and Regulation How the body builds T cells that can recognize almost anything, and keeps them from attacking its own tissues. 29 min

Part II

Cancer and the Immune System

What cancer is, why it is hard for the immune system to detect, and how tumors escape.

2 chapters · about 50 minutes

  1. 6 Chapter 6 Cancer Cells and Tumor Antigens Cancer is evolution within one body. Its cells are almost entirely self, so the immune system must detect the few things about them that are new. 24 min
  2. 7 Chapter 7 Immune Surveillance and Tumor Escape The tumors that reach a doctor are the ones that survived the immune system, and they carry the marks of that selection. 28 min
Interlude 130 Years of Immunotherapy A century of inconsistent results, from Coley’s bacterial toxins onward, then rapid progress after 2010. 1891 2024 13 min · the history, between the science and the medicine

Part III

Immunotherapy

What each kind of treatment does, whom it helps, what it costs and where it falls short.

5 chapters · about 2 hours

  1. 8 Chapter 8 Checkpoint Inhibitors Checkpoint inhibitors do not attack cancer cells; they release brakes on T cells. For a minority of patients, the benefit lasts for years. 27 min
  2. 9 Chapter 9 Therapeutic Antibodies An antibody can only bind. Medicine has turned that one property into five ways to treat cancer. 24 min
  3. 10 Chapter 10 Cell Therapies Medicines that are cells rather than molecules: they multiply inside the patient, kill on contact, and can still be present a decade later. 24 min
  4. 11 Chapter 11 Cancer Vaccines and Oncolytic Viruses The most successful cancer vaccines never show the immune system a cancer cell. The newest are made from the mutations in one patient’s tumor. 27 min
  5. 12 Chapter 12 Resistance and New Directions Why immunotherapy cures some people and does nothing for others, and what researchers are trying next. 27 min

How to read this guide

Built in layers

The main text reads on its own from the first page to the last, and everything else is optional. Each layer can be tried below.

  1. 1

    The main text

    Each chapter is an essay of about 25 minutes that you can read straight through. It does not depend on the extras below.

  2. 2

    Interactive figures

    Each figure shows one idea that is easier to see than to read; you can step through it, drag it or switch between views. This one shows what three kinds of cell display on their surface.

  3. 3

    “Go deeper” boxes

    Molecular names, numbers, history and open debates go in boxes like this one. You can skip them or open every one.

    Go deeper Why “Self & Other”?

    In 1949 the Australian virologists Frank Macfarlane Burnet and Frank Fenner proposed that the body learns, early in life, which molecules are its own, and leaves that “self” alone while attacking what is not. In 1953 Rupert Billingham, Leslie Brent and Peter Medawar showed it in mice: animals given cells from another strain before or just after birth later accepted that strain’s skin grafts as their own.2 Burnet and Medawar shared the 1960 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

    The picture has since grown more complicated. The immune system also reacts to signs of damage and danger, and it tolerates many “others”, from gut bacteria to a growing fetus. Where it draws the line between self and other is the central question of this guide, and a cancer cell is mostly self, with a few new features.

  4. 4

    Glossary

    Every technical word is explained the first time it appears. Dotted words show a short definition when you hover, focus or tap them.

    A T cell inspects the peptides each cell presents on MHC class I. A mutation in a cancer cell can put a neoantigen on display, and a checkpoint inhibitor can release a brake on the T cell that recognizes it.

This guide was researched, written, illustrated and fact-checked by AI (Anthropic’s Claude), working from published research and regulatory documents, with sources for every claim. Mistakes are still possible. It is meant to explain, not to advise; please talk to your care team about any treatment decision.
